text.en: Asha stirred sugar into her tea and saw it vanish. "Solutions are everywhere in daily life," said her teacher.

A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances. The solvent is the medium in which solutes dissolve. It is usually the component in the larger amount. Solutions are classified by physical state (solid, liquid, gas), by the type of solvent such as aqueous solutions, and by the amount of solute as unsaturated, saturated and supersaturated, or concentrated and dilute.
Solubility is the maximum amount that can dissolve in a specified amount of solvent at a given temperature and pressure. It also depends on which solute and solvent are used. Concentration is expressed as mass percentage, volume percentage or other ways.
Hydrated salts, such as copper sulphate and magnesium sulphate, contain water of crystallisation. Hygroscopic substances absorb moisture from the air and deliquescent substances absorb so much that they dissolve.

text.en: If salt is dissolved and the solution is mixed, equal samples from the top and bottom have the same dissolved proportion.

board.text: A uniform mixture has the same composition throughout

text.en: Salt crystals disappear from view as the particles spread through the water. The salt still contributes to the solution’s mass.

board.text: The solute continues to be present

text.en: Sugar dissolved in water forms an aqueous solution. Oil does not mix uniformly with water just because the two were poured together.

board.text: Aqueous means the solvent is water

text.en: Air is a mixture of gases. Saltwater is liquid, and a uniform copper-zinc alloy can be a solid solution.

board.text: Solutions can be solid, liquid or gas

text.en: If forty grams of a substance can dissolve in one hundred grams of water under stated conditions, that number is the solubility for those conditions.

board.text: Solubility tells the maximum amount

text.en: Twenty-five grams dissolved in one hundred grams of water is unsaturated if the limit is forty grams at that temperature.

board.text: Unsaturated means there is room for more

text.en: With forty grams dissolved at the same temperature, the solution is saturated. An extra ten grams stays undissolved at equilibrium.

board.text: Saturated means the limit is reached

text.en: At equilibrium, some particles leave the solid and others return to it. The dissolved amount stays the same overall.

board.text: Dissolved particles can exchange with the solid

text.en: A solution can sometimes temporarily hold more dissolved solute than its usual limit. A disturbance can trigger crystallisation.

board.text: Supersaturated solutions are unstable

text.en: Concentration tells how much solute there is relative to the solution. Saturation compares that amount with the solubility limit.

board.text: Dilute and concentrated compare amounts

text.en: Stirring a solid in water can make it dissolve faster. At the same temperature, it does not increase the equilibrium solubility.

board.text: Stirring can change speed without changing the limit

text.en: Many solid solutes are more soluble in warmer water. Some substances follow a different trend, so use the data for the actual solute.

board.text: Temperature can change the limit

text.en: Many gases are less soluble in water as it gets warmer. Gas that was dissolved can escape as bubbles.

board.text: Warming water can release dissolved gas

text.en: In a sealed soft drink, carbon dioxide pressure helps keep the gas dissolved. Opening the bottle lowers pressure and some gas escapes.

board.text: Higher gas pressure often raises gas solubility

text.en: For a solute in water, add solute mass and water mass first. Then divide solute mass by the total.

board.text: Mass percent divides by total solution mass

text.en: Fifteen grams of solute in one hundred grams of solution is fifteen percent by mass.

board.text: 15 g plus 85 g gives 15% by mass

text.en: If ten millilitres of a liquid solute are used to make one hundred millilitres of solution, the concentration is ten percent by volume.

board.text: Volume percent uses the final solution volume

text.en: Add water to a solution and stir. The original amount of solute is spread through a larger amount of solution, lowering the concentration.

board.text: Dilution adds solvent without adding solute

text.en: A hydrated salt contains water as part of its crystal structure. This water is different from droplets on the outside.

board.text: Water of crystallisation is part of a crystal

text.en: A hydrated copper sulphate crystal contains water in its structure. Its anhydrous form does not have that water of crystallisation.

board.text: Hydrated and anhydrous name different forms

text.en: A moisture absorber can become damp while remaining largely solid. The word hygroscopic describes the tendency to take up moisture.

board.text: Hygroscopic substances take up water from air

text.en: Some solids take up enough water from humid air that the solid dissolves in what it has absorbed. This distinguishes deliquescence.

board.text: A deliquescent solid can form its own solution

text.en: When a hydrated crystal loses water of crystallisation to the surroundings, the process is called efflorescence.

board.text: Some crystals can lose water to drier air

problem.en: 10 g of salt is dissolved in 90 g of water. Find the mass percentage of the solution.

text.en: Mass of solution = 10 + 90 = 100 g.
Mass percentage = (10 / 100) x 100.
So it is 10 percent.

problem.en: At a fixed temperature, 40 g dissolves in 100 g of water. What happens if 50 g is mixed into that water?

text.en: At most 40 g dissolves at the given temperature.

why.en: The solubility data applies to this amount of water.

text.en: The solution is saturated and 10 g remains undissolved.

why.en: Subtract dissolved mass from the initial solute mass.

problem.en: Find the mass percentage when 12 g of solute dissolves in 48 g of water.

text.en: Total mass is 12 + 48 = 60 g.

why.en: The denominator is the mass of the whole solution.
One fifth of the solution mass comes from the solute.

problem.en: What happens to the same solution if another 60 g of water is added?

text.en: The solute stays 12 g while total mass increases to 120 g.

why.en: Adding pure solvent does not add solute.
Doubling total mass halves mass percentage when solute mass is unchanged.

prompt.en: A friend says The solvent is always the substance in the smaller amount. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: The solute is in the smaller amount.
The solvent is in the larger amount.

points.en: Hydrated salts hold water of crystallisation.
